sector: Closed-End Fund / Global Equity Investment Trust
overview: F&C Investment Trust PLC (LSE primary listing: FCIT; NZX secondary listing: FCT.NZ) is a £6.86bn UK closed-end investment trust founded in 1868 - the world's oldest collective investment scheme - managed by Columbia Threadneedle Investments (lead Fund Manager Paul Niven) and a FTSE 100 constituent. It holds a globally diversified portfolio of around 400 individual listed equity positions across multiple regional and thematic sub-strategies, plus a private equity sleeve (~11% of the portfolio via Columbia Threadneedle-sourced buyout funds, Pantheon venture/growth mandates, and Baillie Gifford's Schiehallion), benchmarked against the FTSE All-World Index. FCT.NZ is not a separate company: it is the same GBP-denominated UK vehicle quoted in NZD on the NZX, giving New Zealand investors indirect, unhedged exposure to a sterling-reporting, globally diversified equity portfolio.

business_model.summary: F&C is not an operating company but a pooled investment vehicle. It holds a diversified global equity (plus private equity) portfolio, earns investment income (dividends from underlying holdings, allocated to the 'revenue account') and separately records capital gains/losses on the portfolio (the 'capital account', which dominates total return). Income funds a progressive annual dividend - the 55th consecutive annual increase was declared for 2025 (16.6p total, +6.4%), the 158th consecutive annual dividend payment, fully covered by revenue earned in the year (2025 net revenue return 17.97p/share) and backed by a £125.5m revenue reserve (~1 year of dividend payments). Capital returns (2025: £578.7m capital return vs £86.2m revenue return) are the dominant driver of total shareholder return but are non-recurring and market-dependent. The trust uses modest structural gearing (8.0% effective gearing at FY2025-end, long-dated low-cost loans to 2061 at a blended ~2.4%) to amplify returns, and runs an active discount-control share buyback programme.

revenue_streams.name: Portfolio dividend/investment income (UK + overseas dividends, funds the revenue account and annual dividend)
revenue_streams.trend: growing - FY2025 gross income +1.3% to £113.2m, net revenue +2.0% to £86.2m, a record high; H1-2026 net revenue return per share +8.4% YoY

revenue_streams.name: Capital gains/losses on listed and private equity portfolio (non-recurring, market-driven, dominates total return)
revenue_streams.trend: volatile - FY2025 capital return £578.7m, FY2024 £915.2m, H1-2025 capital return was NEGATIVE (-£52.3m) before a strong H1-2026 (+£722.8m)

business_model.customer_type: Retail and wealth-adviser/platform shareholders on the LSE primary market (UK), plus a small secondary NZX listing (FCT.NZ) attracting NZ retail investors seeking low-cost diversified global equity exposure with a sterling/NZD currency overlay
business_model.geographic_mix: Underlying geographic exposure at 30 Jun 2026: North America ~60%, Europe inc. UK ~19%, Emerging Markets ~10%, Japan ~6%, Developed Pacific ~5%, plus ~11% Private Equity (Schiehallion/Syncona and buyout/venture funds) sitting outside the regional breakdown. Portfolio strategy is built from underweight-vs-benchmark US large-cap exposure (deliberately reduced further in 2026, incl. underweighting the 'Magnificent Seven'), several sub-manager 'sleeves' (JPMorgan large-cap growth, Columbia Threadneedle and Barrow Hanley US value, Invesco emerging markets, Global Focus/Income/Enhanced strategies), and direct/fund-of-fund private equity.

main_competitors: Witan-successor and other AIC 'Global' sector trusts
Global equity index ETFs / passive FTSE All-World and MSCI World trackers
competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest members of the AIC 'Global' sector (~£6.9bn net assets) and a FTSE 100 constituent since 2022 - among the very largest UK-listed investment trusts of any sector. Consistently ranks ahead of the median of both open- and closed-ended global equity peers over 1/3/5/10 years, and its 5-year NAV total return was the strongest of any closed-end peer to end-2025, but this peer-relative strength has not translated into consistently beating its own FTSE All-World benchmark on NAV - FY2025 (+11.6% vs +14.2%) and H1-2026 (+12.4% vs +12.6%) both trailed the index, while FY2024 (+21.0% vs +19.3%) beat it.

moat_factors.description: Ongoing charges of 0.45% (flat 2024-2025, down from 0.79% in 2017) is very low for an actively managed, multi-strategy global equity vehicle with a private equity sleeve; tiered management fee (0.30%/0.25%/0.20% by AUM band, tiers cut further from Jan-2026) falls as the trust grows, a genuine economies-of-scale moat smaller peers cannot replicate.

55 consecutive years of dividend increases (158th consecutive annual payment) as of 2025, with the 56th rise already flagged for 2026 at H1 - a rare, deeply embedded income/growth-hybrid brand credential that anchors demand through periods of relative NAV underperformance and is unmatched in scale by any other UK 'Dividend Hero'.

moat_factors.factor: World's oldest collective investment scheme / heritage brand
moat_factors.description: Founded 1868, longest continuously operating vehicle of its kind, reinforced by industry recognition (Investment Week Investment Company of the Year - Global, 2025) - a durable reputational asset, though it does not by itself generate excess investment returns.

Exposure to ~400 individual listed names plus a differentiated private equity book (Pantheon venture/growth, Schiehallion, buyout funds) not typically available to retail investors via plain index trackers - a genuine structural differentiator, though it has been a performance drag versus the listed benchmark in both FY2024 and FY2025.

£544m of long-term loans extending to 2061 at a blended ~2.4% interest rate, well below prevailing rates, allows the Board to gear (8.0% effective at FY2025) through market cycles without forced selling - a durable structural advantage over open-ended funds and ETFs, though gearing amplifies drawdowns as well as gains.

Scale (£6.9bn) allows meaningful absolute buyback firepower (£96.2m in 2025, £281.5m in 2024, ~1.7-5.3% of capital annually) to narrow the discount, a lever many smaller peers cannot deploy at comparable percentage impact.

weaknesses: NAV total return has trailed its own FTSE All-World benchmark in the two most recent full periods reported (FY2025 +11.6% vs +14.2%; H1-2026 +12.4% vs +12.6%), meaning the trust's active, diversified, multi-sleeve approach has recently underperformed simply buying a world index tracker before fees

Persistent share price discount to NAV (ranged 3.6%-13.8% in 2025, averaged 7.9%; 6.6-6.8% through mid-2026) despite large buybacks - a structural feature of the whole UK investment trust sector since 2022 rather than something F&C can fully control alone

Private equity portfolio (~11% of assets) has lagged the listed global equity benchmark in both FY2024 and FY2025, acting as a performance drag rather than the differentiator it is marketed as during the current period

Fragmented, multi-manager 'sleeve' structure (JPMorgan, Barrow Hanley, Columbia Threadneedle, Invesco, Baillie Gifford/Schiehallion, Pantheon and others) creates governance and accountability complexity and has produced material relative-performance drag from missing a small number of extreme individual stock winners (e.g., Intel, Sandisk, SK Hynix in H1-2026)

Underweight positioning versus the benchmark in the highest-conviction, highest-momentum names (historically the 'Magnificent Seven', more recently top-performing semiconductor/memory names) has been a recurring source of relative underperformance even though it added value in some periods (e.g., FY2025 Mag-7 underweight was additive)

growth_drivers: Continued discount-control share buybacks (£96.2m in FY2025, £41.1m in H1-2026) shrinking the share count and providing modest NAV-per-share accretion, with the Board explicitly targeting a sustainably low, less volatile discount

Fee tier reductions - the 0.25% management fee band now starts at £3.0bn of market cap (down from £3.5bn from Jan-2025, and £4.0bn previously), meaning ongoing charges should continue to fall or stay flat as the trust grows, reinforcing the low-cost moat

4-for-1 share sub-division effective 11 May 2026 (25p shares split into 6.25p shares) intended to improve affordability/liquidity for retail investors, particularly those investing monthly or reinvesting dividends - a demand-side, not value, catalyst but potentially supportive of the discount

Broadening of global equity market leadership beyond the 'Magnificent Seven'/mega-cap US tech (into semiconductors, industrials, energy infrastructure, non-US markets) noted by management in 2025-2026 commentary, which - if sustained - should favour F&C's historically diversified, less mega-cap-concentrated approach relative to the increasingly top-heavy benchmark
Private equity book maturing and potentially closing its performance gap versus listed equities as underlying holdings (e.g., SpaceX/Bending Spoons via Schiehallion) realise value or re-rate

New, lower-cost £100m revolving credit facility (Jun-2026, replacing a matured €42m fixed note) gives flexible, cheap incremental gearing capacity to add market exposure opportunistically, as already demonstrated when futures exposure was increased during the Q2-2026 Iran conflict sell-off

business.description: NAV total return underperformed the FTSE All-World Index in FY2025 (+11.6% vs +14.2%) and H1-2026 (+12.4% vs +12.6%); a diversified, multi-sleeve strategy that persistently trails a simple index tracker on NAV undermines the core value proposition of active management, even though F&C still beats its closed/open-ended peer median.

The ~11% private equity allocation (Pantheon, Schiehallion, Syncona, buyout funds) underperformed the listed benchmark in both FY2024 and FY2025 (though it outperformed listed strategies in H1-2026, +9.1%); valuations rely on Level 3 unobservable inputs and quarterly-lagged third-party marks, adding both return and mark-to-market uncertainty (a 10% fall in the unlisted book would cut net assets by ~1.1% per the H1-2026 disclosure).

business.risk: Multi-sleeve manager structure / stock selection concentration misses
business.description: Relative performance has repeatedly been hurt by the absence of a small number of extreme-performing names (e.g., Intel +284%, Sandisk +872%, SK Hynix +284% in H1-2026) that dominate benchmark returns; the fragmented sub-manager approach increases the chance individual sleeves miss the period's biggest winners even while managing risk well elsewhere.

Board-identified principal risk: the discount ranged 3.6%-13.8% during 2025 alone; a widening discount (as in FY2024, when it moved from 5.9% to 9.2% and cut share price total return to +16.9% versus +21.0% NAV) directly destroys shareholder value independent of underlying portfolio performance and can attract activist attention.

financial.description: Effective gearing of 8.0% (FY2025, at par) and ~4.5-5.7% (H1-2026, at fair value/with derivatives) added value in the rising markets of FY2024-25 and H1-2026, but the same £544m+ of long-term debt plus short-term facilities will magnify NAV losses in a market downturn; the Board's own severe-case viability stress test models a 40% fall in listed and 35% fall in private equity values in 2026.

financial.risk: GBP/NZD currency mismatch for NZX holders
financial.description: FCT.NZ is quoted in NZD but F&C's NAV, dividends and reporting are entirely GBP-denominated (with further layered USD/JPY/EUR exposure from the underlying portfolio - USD weakness cost -6.9% in FY2025 sterling-translated returns). NZ holders bear an additional, unhedged GBP/NZD translation layer on top of the trust's own multi-currency risk, and the NZD share price must track the LSE price plus FX by arbitrage, so NZ investors get no diversification benefit from the separate listing itself.

financial.risk: Currency exposure to USD income and NAV
financial.description: The bulk of the portfolio's dividend income and capital value is USD-denominated; sterling movements against the dollar swing both revenue (FY2025 currency effects cut income by £2.2m) and capital returns materially, and the Board has explicitly flagged that 'a significant weakening of the US Dollar against sterling' is an increased risk given 2025-26 geopolitical volatility.

regulatory.risk: UK cost-disclosure regime transition (Consumer Composite Investments)
regulatory.description: The FCA's new CCI regime replaces PRIIPs/UCITS disclosure from 6 April 2026 (voluntary) with full mandatory adoption by 8 June 2027; while broadly seen as more favourable to investment trusts than the old PRIIPs regime (fixing the double-counting of costs that previously deterred some platforms/advisers from recommending trusts), implementation and comparability risk during the multi-year transition remains a sector overhang, and a 2-Jul-2026 FCA consultation on further simplification adds near-term uncertainty.

F&C must satisfy both UK FCA/Listing Rules/AIC Code governance requirements and NZX Listing Rules for its secondary line; this is a modest incremental compliance cost/risk versus the LSE-only primary listing and has no bearing on underlying portfolio economics.

Board-committed 2050 net zero transition target for the portfolio is a Board-identified principal risk; the portfolio's carbon intensity remains above the benchmark's and the Board acknowledges the path will not be linear, occasionally requiring trade-offs against the primary capital/income return objective.

macro.risk: AI/mega-cap tech capex-cycle and valuation risk
macro.description: An increasing share of both the benchmark's and F&C's relative returns is now driven by a narrow set of AI-infrastructure beneficiaries (semiconductors, memory, hyperscaler capex - ~$700bn in 2026, projected to exceed $1trn in 2027 per management commentary); management itself flags 'growing scrutiny over the likely returns' from this debt-financed capex boom and warns a moderation in spending would remove the earnings support underpinning current market valuations.

FY2025 and H1-2026 were both marked by material geopolitical volatility - US tariff ('Liberation Day') announcements later overturned by the Supreme Court, and the US/Israel-Iran conflict which briefly pushed Brent crude above $100/barrel and disrupted the Strait of Hormuz - directly cited by the Board as an increased and structurally elevated risk to markets, inflation and interest rate paths.

The broader ~£267bn UK closed-end investment trust sector has faced a multi-year de-rating since 2022 driven by wealth-adviser platform outflows toward passive alternatives, historic PRIIPs cost-disclosure distortion, and activist pressure (Saba Capital's UK-wide campaign, including its March-2026 launch of the Saba Capital Investment Trusts UCITS ETF (UKIT) explicitly designed to profit from narrowing discounts across the sector); even F&C's scale and buyback firepower have not eliminated its own discount, which persisted through 2025-26.

Falling policy rates across major central banks have been broadly supportive of equity valuations and cheap refinancing (the new Jun-2026 £100m RCF), but a reacceleration of inflation/rates - a live risk given 2026 oil-price volatility - would pressure both the geared equity portfolio and gearing economics, and could revalue the £544m long-term loan book's market value further below par.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global equity markets reached repeated all-time highs through mid-2026 despite tariff, Middle East and AI-capex-cycle volatility, with an unprecedented scale of hyperscaler capital expenditure (~$700bn in 2026, forecast to exceed $1trn in 2027) the dominant investment theme; leadership has begun to broaden beyond the 'Magnificent Seven' toward semiconductors, memory and AI-infrastructure suppliers, and outside the US into emerging markets and Japan. The UK closed-end investment trust sector (~£267bn) remains in a structural de-rating relative to open-ended funds and ETFs, driven by wealth-adviser platform outflows, historic cost-disclosure distortions (being addressed via the FCA's CCI regime through 2026-2027) and sustained activist pressure (Saba Capital) forcing sector-wide consolidation, tender offers and continuation votes.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - as an ~90%+ invested, modestly geared (~5-8%) global equity vehicle, both NAV and share price are directly cyclical with global equity markets; the portfolio's growing sensitivity to a single dominant macro theme (AI infrastructure capex) increases concentration risk relative to F&C's historically broad, diversified positioning.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - falling policy rates are broadly supportive of equity valuations and reduce the cost of incremental short-term gearing (new Jun-2026 RCF), while the trust's £544m of long-dated, low fixed-rate debt (blended ~2.4% to 2061) becomes relatively more valuable as rates fall, and its market value (below par) is inversely rate-sensitive without affecting cash debt service.
key_input_costs: Investment management fees (0.45% ongoing charges, tiered 0.30%/0.25%/0.20% fee paid to Columbia Threadneedle plus third-party sub-manager fees)
Finance costs on £544m long-term loans, debenture and short-term RCF drawdowns
FX translation (GBP reporting currency vs USD/JPY/EUR underlying holdings and income, plus a further GBP/NZD layer for NZX holders)

recent_developments.event: NAV total return +12.4% for the six months to 30 June 2026, just behind the FTSE All-World benchmark's +12.6%; share price total return +12.8% (discount narrowed marginally from 6.8% to 6.6%). Net revenue return per share rose 8.4% YoY to 2.84p. Underperformance attributed to underweight positions in a small number of extreme-performing semiconductor/memory stocks (Intel, Sandisk, SK Hynix) despite broad-based gains across all listed strategies and private equity (+9.1%).

Four-for-one share sub-division completed 11 May 2026 (each 25p ordinary share split into four 6.25p shares) following AGM shareholder approval, aimed at improving retail affordability/liquidity; all historical per-share and NAV figures restated accordingly (comparatives in this analysis are post-split unless noted).

Repaid a maturing €42m euro-denominated fixed-rate loan note and entered a new £100m unsecured revolving credit facility (expiring Jun-2027); £75m drawn at period-end, used partly to increase market equity exposure via futures during the Q2-2026 Iran-conflict volatility, a trade that proved profitable as markets recovered to new highs.

Board leadership transition: Chair Beatrice Hollond (9 years' tenure) stood down 31 July 2026; James Williams (Non-Executive Chairman of The European Smaller Companies Trust, ex-Schroder Asia Pacific Fund Chairman) succeeded her as Chairman from 1 May 2026 appointment. First interim 2026 dividend of 0.99p declared, flagged as the start of a 56th consecutive annual dividend increase.

FY2025 NAV total return +11.6% underperformed the FTSE All-World Index's +14.2%, but share price total return of +14.6% beat the benchmark as the discount narrowed from 9.2% to 6.8%. 55th consecutive annual dividend increase declared (16.6p total, +6.4%); ongoing charges held flat at 0.45%; won Investment Week Investment Company of the Year - Global 2025. Josh Bottomley (CEO of Dunnhumby) appointed to the Board 1 Sep 2025.

Saba Capital Management continued its multi-year activist campaign against discounted UK investment trusts sector-wide, launching the Saba Capital Investment Trusts UCITS ETF (ticker UKIT/UK1T) in March 2026, explicitly designed to profit from narrowing discounts across the ~£267bn closed-end fund sector - keeping discount-control and governance pressure elevated industry-wide, including for F&C.

FCA published its final Consumer Composite Investments (CCI) rules (PS25/20), replacing the PRIIPs/UCITS disclosure regime with a framework more favourable to closed-end funds' true cost presentation; voluntary adoption from 6 April 2026, full mandatory adoption by 8 June 2027 - a long-awaited fix for a distortion that had previously deterred some adviser/platform recommendations of investment trusts including F&C.

guidance.as_of: H1-2026 Half-Year Report (3 August 2026) and FY2025 Annual Report (16 March 2026)

items.target: another increase, to be the 56th consecutive annual rise (FY2025 total was 16.6p pre-split / 4.15p post-split-equivalent)
items.vs_prior: maintained (continuation of the progressive dividend policy)
items.notes: First interim of 0.99p declared for 2026 (paid 3 Aug 2026); Chairman explicitly stated the Board 'plans to deliver another rise in our total dividend for this year, which will be the 56th consecutive annual rise', funded if needed by the £136.6m revenue reserve at H1-2026.

items.target: sustainably low deviation between share price and NAV, reduced discount volatility (no specific numeric target disclosed)
items.notes: Discount narrowed from 9.2% (start of 2025) to 6.8% (end of 2025) to 6.6% (H1-2026); Board continues an active buyback programme (£96.2m FY2025, £41.1m H1-2026) as its primary tool, alongside monitoring absolute level and volatility versus peers/sector.

items.target: no explicit forward numeric target; maintained broadly in the mid-single-digit to high-single-digit percent range
items.notes: Effective gearing (debt at fair value) fell from 4.7% at start of 2026 to 4.5% at H1-2026 (5.7% including derivatives); FY2025 effective gearing (at par) was 8.0%, down from 8.6%. New £100m RCF (Jun-2026) provides flexible incremental capacity.

items.target: no explicit forward numeric target; management fee tier thresholds continue to step down (0.25% band now applies above £3.0bn from Jan-2026, down from £3.5bn)
items.notes: FY2025 ongoing charges were 0.45%, flat versus FY2024 and down from 0.79% in 2017; fee-tier reductions imply continued downward or flat cost pressure as the trust's market cap grows.

items.target: continued diversification, further reduction in US/mega-cap tech concentration, increased emerging markets weighting
items.vs_prior: changed - directional shift, no numeric target
items.notes: Management stated it has 'been modestly reducing exposure to US assets in recent years, to US large cap growth stocks in particular, and increasing our allocation elsewhere, notably to emerging markets', reflecting a view that market leadership will continue to broaden beyond recent winners.

guidance.management_commentary: Chairman James Williams-era commentary (via outgoing Chair Beatrice Hollond, 31 July 2026) and Fund Manager Paul Niven (31 July 2026) both stressed continued conviction in the diversified, multi-sleeve approach despite recent narrow, AI-driven market leadership, noting F&C 'outperform[ed] the median return of our peers in NAV and share price return terms over the first half as well as over one, three, five and ten years' even while trailing its own benchmark. Management flagged two key forward risks: (1) an unresolved and fragile geopolitical backdrop (Middle East, US tariff/trade policy) creating a 'changed world order' with less policy clarity/consistency, and (2) 'growing scrutiny over the likely returns' from debt-financed AI infrastructure capex, warning that a moderation in that spending would remove the earnings support currently underpinning market valuations. No formal profit forecast is given; the Board's ten-year long-term viability stress test (to 2035) models net assets falling to a floor of £1.6bn under a severe 40%/35% listed/private-equity drawdown scenario before recovering, versus a base case that assumes no change to the progressive dividend policy.

bull_case: Exceptionally low-cost (0.45% ongoing charges) access to a genuinely diversified, actively managed global equity and private equity portfolio, with a scale-driven fee structure (tiered management fee bands stepping down further with growth) that few peers can replicate

55 consecutive years of dividend increases (56th flagged for 2026) backed by a substantial and growing revenue reserve (£136.6m at H1-2026), fully covered by revenue income, offering a rare combination of income growth and capital growth that has compounded to a 10.4% p.a. 20-year shareholder total return

Active, well-resourced discount-control buyback programme (£96.2m FY2025, £41.1m H1-2026) has structurally narrowed the discount from 9.2% (early 2025) to 6.6% (mid-2026), directly accretive to NAV per share and providing a lever to keep closing the gap toward the wider FCA CCI cost-disclosure reform tailwind for the sector

Consistent peer-relative outperformance - F&C has beaten the median return of both open- and closed-ended global equity peers over 1/3/5/10 years, and its 5-year NAV return was the strongest of any closed-end peer to end-2025, evidencing a durable, repeatable process even in periods of benchmark-relative underperformance

Deliberate diversification away from US mega-cap tech concentration (increasing emerging markets and non-US exposure) positions the trust to benefit disproportionately if the broadening of market leadership beyond the 'Magnificent Seven'/AI infrastructure narrative - already visible in H1-2026 - continues, reducing single-theme concentration risk relative to an increasingly top-heavy benchmark
bear_case: F&C's NAV total return has underperformed its own FTSE All-World benchmark in the two most recently reported periods (FY2025 +11.6% vs +14.2%; H1-2026 +12.4% vs +12.6%), meaning a NZ investor could have captured more return, more cheaply, by simply buying a global index tracker - the central unresolved tension in the investment case

The private equity allocation (~11% of assets), marketed as a differentiator, has lagged the listed benchmark in both FY2024 and FY2025, relies on lagged/Level-3 valuations, and adds illiquidity and mark-to-market uncertainty without (so far) delivering the outperformance that would justify the added complexity and cost

Persistent share price discount to NAV (6.6-6.8% through mid-2026, having ranged as high as 13.8% in 2025) despite large, sustained buybacks reflects both F&C-specific skepticism and a structural, sector-wide UK investment trust de-rating (wealth-adviser outflows, historic cost-disclosure distortion, Saba Capital activism) that management cannot fully control and that could persist or widen again in a risk-off environment

8% effective gearing and multi-sleeve, moderately concentrated growth/tech exposure (via semiconductor and AI-infrastructure beneficiaries within several strategies) leave the trust structurally exposed to a reversal in the AI capex cycle or a broader equity market drawdown, which would be amplified - not cushioned - by the fund's leverage, with the Board's own worst-case stress test modelling a 40% listed equity fall in 2026

For NZX-listed holders specifically: FCT.NZ is a small, arbitrage-priced secondary listing that adds an unhedged GBP/NZD currency layer on top of the trust's own USD/EUR/JPY exposure, offers no diversification benefit versus simply holding FCIT.L, provides no NZ imputation credits on UK-sourced dividends, and is subject to NZ FIF/FDR tax treatment that will diverge from the trust's own reported total returns for most NZ retail investors
investment_thesis: F&C Investment Trust is a genuinely differentiated, ultra-low-cost (0.45% OCR), 158-year dividend-payment/55-year dividend-growth compounder with a credible long-run (10- and 20-year) track record of beating both its peer group and, over longer horizons, its own benchmark - but it is fundamentally a modestly levered, actively managed global equity index proxy, and in the two most recent reporting periods (FY2025 and H1-2026) it has underperformed the plain FTSE All-World benchmark on NAV. For a New Zealand investor accessing it via the small, arbitrage-priced FCT.NZ secondary line (adding an unhedged GBP/NZD layer, no imputation credits, and FIF/FDR tax treatment on top of the trust's own currency and market risk), the only durable sources of return above a low-cost world index tracker are: (a) the still-wide, sector-structural discount to NAV closing further (from ~6.6% toward zero, aided by ongoing buybacks and the FCA's more favourable CCI cost-disclosure regime), (b) the ~11% private equity book eventually delivering the outperformance it has so far failed to produce, and (c) continued buyback-driven NAV-per-share accretion. Absent one or more of those, F&C is a lower-returning, higher-cost, currency- and gearing-amplified way to own the same global equity beta available directly and more cheaply through a passive index fund.
